## Session 8 — Generalized eigenvalue problems and numerical spectral methods {#sec-module-c-session-8}

The final session connects inner-product geometry directly to the Numerical Linear Algebra and HASC topics that motivated the curriculum.

Our main ideas are generalized self-adjointness, spectral projections, Rayleigh–Ritz approximation, and polynomial filtering.

### Why generalized eigenvalue problems arise {#sec-module-c-session-8-why-generalized-eigenvalue-problems-arise}

In elementary linear algebra, an eigenvalue problem has the form

$$
Ax=\lambda x.
$$

But numerical methods for PDEs often produce a generalized eigenvalue problem

$$
\boxed{ Kx=\lambda Mx, }
$$

where $K$ and $M$ are matrices arising from bilinear forms.

For example, in a finite-element discretization of

$$
-u''=\lambda u
$$

with homogeneous Dirichlet conditions, one obtains

$$
K_{ij}=\int_0^1\phi_j'(x)\phi_i'(x)\,dx,
$$

and

$$
M_{ij}=\int_0^1\phi_j(x)\phi_i(x)\,dx.
$$

Here $K$ is a stiffness matrix and $M$ is a mass matrix.

Both are symmetric, and in the standard conforming Dirichlet setting they are SPD.

The matrix $M$ is the Gram matrix of the basis with respect to the $L^2$ inner product.

Thus generalized eigenvalue problems arise naturally when different bilinear forms describe different aspects of the underlying function-space geometry.

### Transforming the generalized problem {#sec-module-c-session-8-transforming-the-generalized-problem}

Assume $M$ is SPD.

We can rewrite

$$
Kx=\lambda Mx
$$

as

$$
\boxed{ M^{-1}Kx=\lambda x. }
$$

Define

$$
T=M^{-1}K.
$$

The matrix $T$ need not be symmetric in ordinary Euclidean coordinates.

However, it is self-adjoint with respect to the $M$-inner product.

Let's prove this.

For $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
  \langle Tx,y\rangle_M &=(M^{-1}Kx)^TMy\\
  &=x^TK^Ty\\
  &=x^TKy,
\end{aligned}
$$

since $K=K^T$.

On the other hand,

$$
\begin{aligned}
  \langle x,Ty\rangle_M &=x^TM(M^{-1}Ky)\\
  &=x^TKy.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{ \langle Tx,y\rangle_M = \langle x,Ty\rangle_M. }
$$

Thus $T$ is self-adjoint in the $M$-geometry.

This explains why generalized symmetric eigenvalue problems retain the favorable spectral properties of ordinary symmetric problems.

### Orthogonality of generalized eigenvectors {#sec-module-c-session-8-orthogonality-of-generalized-eigenvectors}

Suppose

$$
Kv_i=\lambda_iMv_i,
$$

$$
Kv_j=\lambda_jMv_j.
$$

Multiply the first equation by $v_j^T$:

$$
v_j^TKv_i = \lambda_i v_j^TMv_i.
$$

Similarly,

$$
v_i^TKv_j = \lambda_j v_i^TMv_j.
$$

Because $K$ and $M$ are symmetric, the left-hand sides agree, and so do the $M$-inner products.

Thus

$$
(\lambda_i-\lambda_j)v_i^TMv_j=0.
$$

If $\lambda_i\ne\lambda_j$,

$$
\boxed{ v_i^TMv_j=0. }
$$

Therefore generalized eigenvectors associated with distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal in the $M$-inner product.

They need not be orthogonal in the ordinary Euclidean inner product.

This is exactly the distinction between intrinsic geometric structure and coordinate representation developed earlier in the module.

### The generalized Rayleigh quotient {#sec-module-c-session-8-the-generalized-rayleigh-quotient}

For a nonzero vector $x$, define

$$
\boxed{ \rho_{K,M}(x) = \frac{x^TKx}{x^TMx}. }
$$

Because $M$ is SPD,

$$
x^TMx>0.
$$

If $x$ is a generalized eigenvector,

$$
Kx=\lambda Mx,
$$

then

$$
\rho_{K,M}(x)=\lambda.
$$

More generally, the quotient plays the same role as the ordinary Rayleigh quotient, but in the geometry defined by $M$.

If $K$ is symmetric and $M$ is SPD, the generalized eigenvalues are real, and the extreme values satisfy variational characterizations analogous to the ordinary symmetric case.

This is particularly important in finite-element eigenvalue problems.

### Rayleigh–Ritz approximation {#sec-module-c-session-8-rayleigh-ritz-approximation}

Suppose $A=A^T\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a $k$-dimensional trial subspace with orthonormal basis columns

$$
Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}, \qquad Q^TQ=I.
$$

We seek an approximate eigenvector $v\in U$.

Write

$$
v=Qy.
$$

The Rayleigh–Ritz method constructs the smaller matrix

$$
\boxed{H=Q^TAQ.}
$$

We then solve

$$
Hy=\theta y.
$$

The scalar $\theta$ is a **Ritz value**, and

$$
v=Qy
$$

is a **Ritz vector**.

#### Where does this reduced eigenproblem come from? {#module-c-session-8-rayleigh-ritz-approximation-where-does-this-reduced-eigenproblem-come-from}

We would like the residual

$$
r=Av-\theta v
$$

to vanish.

But because $v$ is restricted to the trial subspace, we generally cannot achieve $r=0$.

Instead, impose the condition

$$
\boxed{r\perp U.}
$$

Since the columns of $Q$ span $U$, this is equivalent to

$$
Q^Tr=0.
$$

Substituting $v=Qy$,

$$
Q^T(AQy-\theta Qy)=0.
$$

Therefore,

$$
Q^TAQy=\theta Q^TQy.
$$

Since $Q^TQ=I$,

$$
\boxed{ Q^TAQy=\theta y. }
$$

This is exactly the projected eigenvalue problem.

**Rayleigh–Ritz approximation arises by requiring the eigenpair residual to be orthogonal to the trial subspace.**

This is closely related to Galerkin orthogonality for PDE approximation.

Both methods project an infinite- or high-dimensional problem onto a smaller trial space and impose an orthogonality condition on the residual.

### Generalized Rayleigh–Ritz approximation {#sec-module-c-session-8-generalized-rayleigh-ritz-approximation}

For

$$
Kx=\lambda Mx,
$$

choose a trial subspace with basis columns $Q$.

Seek

$$
v=Qy.
$$

The generalized residual is

$$
r=KQy-\theta MQy.
$$

Impose

$$
Q^Tr=0.
$$

Then

$$
\boxed{ Q^TKQy=\theta Q^TMQy. }
$$

Thus Rayleigh–Ritz produces a smaller generalized eigenvalue problem.

If the columns of $Q$ are $M$-orthonormal, so that

$$
Q^TMQ=I,
$$

the equation simplifies to

$$
\boxed{ Q^TKQy=\theta y. }
$$

The requirement $Q^Tr=0$ means that the residual vector represents the zero functional on the trial subspace under the ordinary coordinate pairing. Equivalently, the operator residual

$$
M^{-1}r
$$

is $M$-orthogonal to the trial subspace.

This is a direct application of the weighted inner-product theory.

### Polynomial filtering and self-adjoint spectral theory {#sec-module-c-session-8-polynomial-filtering-and-self-adjoint-spectral-theory}

Suppose $A$ is Hermitian.

The spectral theorem gives

$$
A=Q\Lambda Q^H.
$$

For a polynomial $p$,

$$
\boxed{ p(A)=Qp(\Lambda)Q^H. }
$$

To understand this, note that

$$
A^k=Q\Lambda^kQ^H.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
  p(A) &=\sum_{j=0}^d a_jA^j\\
  &=Q\left(\sum_{j=0}^d a_j\Lambda^j\right)Q^H\\
  &=Qp(\Lambda)Q^H.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, for an eigenvector $q_i$,

$$
p(A)q_i=p(\lambda_i)q_i.
$$

A polynomial of the operator preserves the eigendirections and changes the scaling associated with each eigenvalue.

This is the fundamental mechanism of polynomial spectral filtering.

### Why Chebyshev polynomials are useful {#sec-module-c-session-8-why-chebyshev-polynomials-are-useful}

Chebyshev polynomials have controlled behavior on $[-1,1]$.

The first-kind Chebyshev polynomials satisfy

$$
T_0(t)=1,\qquad T_1(t)=t,
$$

and the recurrence

$$
\boxed{ T_{k+1}(t)=2tT_k(t)-T_{k-1}(t). }
$$

For $t\in[-1,1]$,

$$
|T_k(t)|\le1.
$$

Outside that interval, their magnitude can grow rapidly with $k$.

Suppose the unwanted eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix lie in an interval $[a,b]$.

Map that interval to $[-1,1]$ using

$$
s(t)=\frac{2t-(a+b)}{b-a}.
$$

Then a filter of the form

$$
p_k(t)=T_k(s(t))
$$

is bounded in magnitude by $1$ on the unwanted interval, while it can grow substantially at desired eigenvalues outside that interval.

After suitable scaling or normalization, this can create strong relative amplification of desired spectral components.

The operator filter is

$$
p_k(A)=T_k\left(\frac{2A-(a+b)I}{b-a}\right).
$$

In practice, we generally do not form this matrix polynomial explicitly.

Instead, we apply the Chebyshev recurrence to vectors or blocks of vectors.

This allows high-degree polynomial filtering using repeated matrix-vector or matrix-block products.

### Connection to HASC and hardware-aware computing {#sec-module-c-session-8-connection-to-hasc-and-hardware-aware-computing}

The underlying mathematical structure explains why Chebyshev-filtered subspace iteration is effective.

A Hermitian matrix has an orthonormal eigenbasis.

Polynomial functions of that matrix act diagonally on its spectral components.

Orthogonalization keeps the evolving trial basis well-conditioned.

Rayleigh–Ritz extracts approximate eigenpairs from the trial subspace.

Residuals measure how far the approximate eigenpairs are from satisfying the original eigenproblem.

From a numerical perspective, however, we must distinguish exact arithmetic from finite-precision computation.

In floating-point arithmetic, matrix-vector products, polynomial recurrences, and orthogonalization steps introduce errors.

These errors may alter convergence behavior, especially when the desired spectral components are weak, eigenvalues are clustered, or a polynomial recurrence strongly amplifies some directions.

This creates the mathematical setting for questions in hardware-aware scientific computing: how should one balance arithmetic precision, communication costs, memory bandwidth, numerical stability, and the accuracy required for convergence?

The tools developed in Module C provide the geometric language needed to analyze those questions.

| Mathematical concept                  | Role in an eigenvalue algorithm                     |
| ------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| Self-adjointness                      | Real spectrum and orthogonal spectral decomposition |
| Orthogonal projection                 | Approximation within trial subspaces                |
| Rayleigh quotient                     | Eigenvalue estimates                                |
| Rayleigh–Ritz                         | Extraction of approximate eigenpairs                |
| Adjoint identities                    | Residual orthogonality and projected equations      |
| Positive definiteness                 | Weighted geometry and generalized eigenproblems     |
| Spectral theorem                      | Justification of polynomial filtering               |
| Condition numbers and singular values | Sensitivity and finite-precision behavior           |

The detailed convergence and stability analysis belongs to Modules D and E.

### Exercise 10 — Structural synthesis {#module-c-exercise-10}

explain the logical relationship among the following ideas:

V/\ker T\cong\operatorname{im}T.
$$

Explain which results are purely algebraic and which depend on an inner product.

Finally, explain why the restriction

$$
T|_{(\ker T)^\perp}: (\ker T)^\perp\to\operatorname{im}T
$$

is an isomorphism in finite dimensions, and whether it must be an isometry.

## Worked solutions {#sec-module-c-worked-solutions}

### Solution 1 — Weighted geometry {#module-c-solution-1}

The matrix $G$ is symmetric.

Its eigenvalues are $3$ and $1$, both positive.

Therefore $G$ is SPD, and

$$
\langle x,y\rangle_G=x^TGy
$$

is an inner product.

Now let $x=(1,0)^T$ and $y=(y_1,y_2)^T$.

Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
  \langle x,y\rangle_G &= \begin{pmatrix}
  1&0
\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}
  2&1\\
  1&2
\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}
  y_1\\
  y_2
\end{pmatrix}\\
&=2y_1+y_2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $x\perp_G y$ if and only if

$$
2y_1+y_2=0.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{ x^{\perp_G} = \operatorname{span}\{(1,-2)^T\}. }
$$

By contrast, the Euclidean orthogonal complement of $x$ is

$$
x^\perp=\operatorname{span}\{(0,1)^T\}.
$$

The difference occurs because orthogonality depends on the chosen inner product.

### Solution 2 — Weighted Riesz representative {#module-c-solution-2}

The functional has coefficient column

$$
c=\begin{pmatrix}
  3\\
  0
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Its Riesz representative satisfies

$$
Ga_f=c.
$$

Since

$$
G^{-1} = \frac13 \begin{pmatrix}
  2&-1\\
  -1&2
\end{pmatrix},
$$

we obtain

$$
a_f = G^{-1}c = \boxed{ \begin{pmatrix}
  2\\
  -1
\end{pmatrix}. }
$$

Verification:

$$
Ga_f= \begin{pmatrix}
  2&1\\
  1&2
\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}
  2\\
  -1
\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}
  3\\
  0
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\langle x,a_f\rangle_G =x^TGa_f =3x_1=f(x).
$$

The norm of the representative is

$$
\begin{aligned}
  \|a_f\|_G^2 &=a_f^TGa_f\\
  &= \begin{pmatrix}
  2&-1
\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}
  3\\
  0
\end{pmatrix}\\
&=6.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus

$$
\boxed{ \|a_f\|_G=\sqrt6. }
$$

By the Riesz isometry theorem,

$$
\boxed{\|f\|_{V^*}=\sqrt6.}
$$

### Solution 3 — Weighted adjoint {#module-c-solution-3}

We use

$$
A^{*_{G_V,G_W}} = G_V^{-1}A^TG_W.
$$

First,

$$
A^TG_W = \begin{pmatrix}
  1&0\\
  2&1
\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}
  1&0\\
  0&3
\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}
  1&0\\
  2&3
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Also,

$$
G_V^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}
  1/2&0\\
  0&1
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{ A^{*_{G_V,G_W}} = \begin{pmatrix}
  1/2&0\\
  2&3
\end{pmatrix}. }
$$

Now take $x=(1,2)^T$, $y=(3,1)^T$.

We have

$$
Ax=(5,2)^T.
$$

Thus

$$
\langle Ax,y\rangle_{G_W} = \begin{pmatrix}
  5&2
\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}
  1&0\\
  0&3
\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}
  3\\
  1
\end{pmatrix} =21.
$$

On the other side,

$$
A^{*_{G_V,G_W}}y = \begin{pmatrix}
  3/2\\
  9
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\langle x,A^{*_{G_V,G_W}}y\rangle_{G_V} = \begin{pmatrix}
  1&2
\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}
  2&0\\
  0&1
\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}
  3/2\\
  9
\end{pmatrix} =21.
$$

The defining identity holds.

The ordinary transpose is not the correct adjoint because the inner products are not Euclidean.

### Solution 4 — Orthogonal versus oblique projections {#module-c-solution-4}

The subspace $U$ has basis vector

$$
u=(1,1)^T.
$$

The Euclidean orthogonal projection is

$$
P_U=\frac{uu^T}{u^Tu} = \boxed{ \frac12 \begin{pmatrix}
  1&1\\
  1&1
\end{pmatrix}. }
$$

For $x=(2,0)^T$,

$$
P_Ux=(1,1)^T.
$$

Its distance from $x$ is

$$
\|x-P_Ux\| = \|(1,-1)\| = \sqrt2.
$$

Now project onto $U$ along

$$
W=\operatorname{span}\{(0,1)^T\}.
$$

Every vector decomposes as

$$
(x_1,x_2) = (x_1,x_1)+(0,x_2-x_1).
$$

Therefore the oblique projection is

$$
Q(x_1,x_2)=(x_1,x_1),
$$

with matrix

$$
\boxed{ Q= \begin{pmatrix}
  1&0\\
  1&0
\end{pmatrix}. }
$$

Then

$$
Qx=(2,2)^T.
$$

Its distance from $x$ is

$$
\|x-Qx\|=2.
$$

Thus

$$
\sqrt2<2,
$$

confirming that the orthogonal projection is closer.

Both satisfy

$$
P_U^2=P_U,\qquad Q^2=Q.
$$

But

$$
P_U^T=P_U,
$$

while

$$
Q^T\ne Q.
$$

### Solution 5 — SPD matrix and Rayleigh quotient {#module-c-solution-5}

For

$$
A= \begin{pmatrix}
  2&1\\
  1&2
\end{pmatrix},
$$

the characteristic polynomial is

$$
\det(A-\lambda I) =(2-\lambda)^2-1.
$$

Its roots are

$$
\boxed{\lambda_1=1,\qquad\lambda_2=3.}
$$

Corresponding orthonormal eigenvectors are

$$
q_1=\frac1{\sqrt2}(1,-1)^T,
$$

$$
q_2=\frac1{\sqrt2}(1,1)^T.
$$

Since $A$ is symmetric and both eigenvalues are positive, it is SPD.

The Rayleigh quotient satisfies

$$
\boxed{ 1\le\rho_A(x)\le3. }
$$

The minimum and maximum are attained at $q_1$ and $q_2$, respectively.

For $x=(1,0)^T$,

$$
\rho_A(x) = \frac{x^TAx}{x^Tx} = \boxed{2}.
$$

### Solution 6 — Rank-deficient least squares {#module-c-solution-6}

The columns of $A$ are identical:

$$
a_1=a_2=(1,2)^T.
$$

Thus

$$
\operatorname{im}A=\operatorname{span}\{(1,2)^T\}.
$$

The orthogonal projection of $b=(1,0)^T$ onto this line is

$$
P_{\operatorname{im}A}b = \frac{(1,2)^Tb}{(1,2)^T(1,2)}(1,2)^T.
$$

Since

$$
(1,2)^Tb=1,\qquad (1,2)^T(1,2)=5,
$$

we obtain

$$
\boxed{ P_{\operatorname{im}A}b = \begin{pmatrix}
  1/5\\
  2/5
\end{pmatrix}. }
$$

But

$$
Ax=(x_1+x_2)(1,2)^T.
$$

Therefore every least-squares minimizer satisfies

$$
x_1+x_2=\frac15.
$$

The full solution family is

$$
\boxed{ x= \begin{pmatrix}
  1/10\\
  1/10
\end{pmatrix} +t\begin{pmatrix}
  1\\
  -1
\end{pmatrix}. }
$$

The kernel is

$$
\ker A=\operatorname{span}\{(1,-1)^T\}.
$$

Its orthogonal complement is

$$
(\ker A)^\perp = \operatorname{span}\{(1,1)^T\}.
$$

The minimum-norm solution must lie in this orthogonal complement.

Therefore its two coordinates must be equal.

Together with $x_1+x_2=1/5$, this gives

$$
\boxed{ x_{\min}= \begin{pmatrix}
  1/10\\
  1/10
\end{pmatrix}. }
$$

### Solution 7 — Finite-element stiffness matrix {#module-c-solution-7}

For continuous piecewise-linear hat functions on a uniform mesh with spacing $h=1/3$, each interior basis function has derivative magnitude $1/h=3$ on its two adjacent elements.

Therefore,

$$
a(\phi_i,\phi_i) = 2h\left(\frac1h\right)^2 = \frac2h=6.
$$

The two neighboring basis functions overlap on one element, where their derivatives have opposite signs.

Thus

$$
a(\phi_1,\phi_2) = -h\left(\frac1h\right)^2 = -\frac1h=-3.
$$

Hence

$$
\boxed{ K= \begin{pmatrix}
  6&-3\\
  -3&6
\end{pmatrix}. }
$$

Each hat function has area $h=1/3$, so for forcing $f=1$,

$$
\boxed{ b=\begin{pmatrix}
  1/3\\
  1/3
\end{pmatrix}. }
$$

Solving gives

$$
\boxed{ c=\begin{pmatrix}
  1/9\\
  1/9
\end{pmatrix}. }
$$

To prove that $K$ is SPD structurally, let

$$
v_h=c_1\phi_1+c_2\phi_2.
$$

Then

$$
c^TKc=\int_0^1|v_h'(x)|^2\,dx.
$$

This is nonnegative.

If it equals zero, $v_h'=0$ almost everywhere, so $v_h$ is constant.

Because $v_h$ vanishes at both endpoints, it must be identically zero.

Independence of the basis functions implies $c=0$.

Therefore $c^TKc>0$ for every nonzero $c$, proving positive definiteness.

### Solution 8 — Generalized eigenvalues {#module-c-solution-8}

The generalized eigenvalue equation is

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
  2&0\\
  0&6
\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}
  x_1\\
  x_2
\end{pmatrix} = \lambda \begin{pmatrix}
  2&0\\
  0&1
\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}
  x_1\\
  x_2
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The two equations are

$$
2x_1=2\lambda x_1,
$$

$$
6x_2=\lambda x_2.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{\lambda_1=1,\qquad\lambda_2=6.}
$$

We have

$$
T=M^{-1}K = \begin{pmatrix}
  1&0\\
  0&6
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

It is self-adjoint in the $M$-inner product because

$$
T^TM=MT=K.
$$

An $M$-orthonormal eigenbasis is

$$
q_1=\frac1{\sqrt2}(1,0)^T, \qquad q_2=(0,1)^T.
$$

Indeed,

$$
q_i^TMq_j=\delta_{ij}.
$$

For $x=c_1q_1+c_2q_2$,

$$
x^TMx=c_1^2+c_2^2,
$$

and

$$
x^TKx=c_1^2+6c_2^2.
$$

Thus

$$
\boxed{ \rho_{K,M}(x) = \frac{c_1^2+6c_2^2}{c_1^2+c_2^2}. }
$$

This is a weighted average of the generalized eigenvalues.

### Solution 9 — Dense but nonclosed range {#module-c-solution-9}

For $x\in\ell^2$,

$$
\|Tx\|_{\ell^2}^2 = \sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{|x_n|^2}{n^2} \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty|x_n|^2 = \|x\|_{\ell^2}^2.
$$

Thus $T$ is bounded, with $\|T\|\le1$.

It is injective because

$$
Tx=0\implies x_n/n=0\quad\forall n,
$$

so $x=0$.

It is self-adjoint because

$$
\langle Tx,y\rangle = \sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{x_ny_n}{n} = \langle x,Ty\rangle.
$$

Every finitely supported sequence belongs to the image: if $y$ has only finitely many nonzero entries, choose $x_n=ny_n$.

Since finitely supported sequences are dense in $\ell^2$, the image is dense.

However, consider

$$
y=\left(1,\frac12,\frac13,\ldots\right).
$$

We have

$$
\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac1{n^2}<\infty,
$$

so $y\in\ell^2$.

If $Tx=y$, then

$$
x_n=ny_n=1
$$

for every $n$.

But $(1,1,\ldots)\notin\ell^2$.

Therefore $y\notin\operatorname{im}T$.

Its finite truncations do belong to the image and converge to $y$, so the image is not closed.

Since $\ker T=\{0\}$,

$$
(\ker T)^\perp=\ell^2.
$$

But

$$
\operatorname{im}T\ne\ell^2.
$$

Hence

$$
\boxed{ \operatorname{im}T\ne(\ker T)^\perp, \qquad \overline{\operatorname{im}T}=(\ker T)^\perp. }
$$

This demonstrates why closures matter in infinite-dimensional operator theory.

### Solution 10 — Structural synthesis {#module-c-solution-10}

The identity

$$
\operatorname{im}T^\vee=(\ker T)^0
$$

is purely algebraic.

It concerns the algebraic dual map and annihilator, neither of which requires an inner product.

Once inner products are chosen, the Riesz representation theorem identifies the dual spaces with the original spaces.

Under these identifications,

$$
T^\vee
$$

corresponds to the adjoint $T^*$, and

$$
(\ker T)^0
$$

corresponds to

$$
(\ker T)^\perp.
$$

Thus

$$
\boxed{ \operatorname{im}T^*=(\ker T)^\perp }
$$

in finite dimensions.

The orthogonal decomposition theorem gives

$$
\boxed{ V=\ker T\oplus^\perp(\ker T)^\perp = \ker T\oplus^\perp\operatorname{im}T^*. }
$$

Independently, the first isomorphism theorem gives

$$
\boxed{ V/\ker T\cong\operatorname{im}T. }
$$

The inner product allows us to identify the quotient with the orthogonal complement of the kernel:

$$
V/\ker T\cong(\ker T)^\perp.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{ T|_{(\ker T)^\perp}: (\ker T)^\perp\to\operatorname{im}T }
$$

is an isomorphism.

It is injective because its kernel is

$$
(\ker T)^\perp\cap\ker T=\{0\}.
$$

It is surjective because every $v\in V$ decomposes as

$$
v=k+u, \qquad k\in\ker T,\quad u\in(\ker T)^\perp,
$$

and

$$
Tv=Tu.
$$

However, the restriction need not be an isometry.

It preserves vector-space structure but may change lengths.

For example, multiplication by $2$ on $\mathbb R$ is an isomorphism whose kernel is zero, but

$$
\|2x\|=2\|x\|.
$$

Thus the structural isomorphism theorem does not imply preservation of geometric distances.

## Computational laboratory — MATLAB {#sec-module-c-computational-laboratory-matlab}

This laboratory is designed to make the mathematical relationships concrete.

Each experiment corresponds to one or more sessions. The calculations use small matrices for which the theoretical results can also be verified by hand.

The code is intended to run as a MATLAB script.

```matlab
%% Module C — Inner-Product Geometry
clear; clc;

%% 1. Riesz representation in a weighted inner product
G = [2 1;
     1 2];

% Functional f(x) = 3*x1
c = [3; 0];

% Riesz representative: G*a = c
a = G \ c;

x = [1; 2];

fprintf('Riesz representative:\n');
disp(a);

fprintf('Functional value: %.8f\n', c.'*x);
fprintf('Inner-product value: %.8f\n', x.'*G*a);

fprintf('Functional norm: %.8f\n', ...
    sqrt(c.'*(G\c)));

fprintf('Representative norm: %.8f\n', ...
    sqrt(a.'*G*a));


%% 2. Adjoint with weighted inner products
A = [1 2;
     0 1];

Gv = diag([2, 1]);
Gw = diag([1, 3]);

% Adjoint matrix: Gv^{-1} * A^T * Gw
A_adj = Gv \ (A.'*Gw);

x = [1; 2];
y = [3; 1];

left  = (A*x).'*Gw*y;
right = x.'*Gv*(A_adj*y);

fprintf('Weighted adjoint error: %.3e\n', ...
    abs(left-right));


%% 3. Orthogonal and oblique projections
u = [1; 1];

P_orth = (u*u.')/(u.'*u);

% Projection onto span(u) along span(e2)
P_oblique = [1 0;
             1 0];

x = [2; 0];

fprintf('Orthogonal projection:\n');
disp(P_orth*x);

fprintf('Oblique projection:\n');
disp(P_oblique*x);

fprintf('Orthogonal distance: %.8f\n', ...
    norm(x-P_orth*x));

fprintf('Oblique distance: %.8f\n', ...
    norm(x-P_oblique*x));

fprintf('||P_orth^2-P_orth|| = %.3e\n', ...
    norm(P_orth^2-P_orth));

fprintf('||P_orth^T-P_orth|| = %.3e\n', ...
    norm(P_orth.'-P_orth));


%% 4. Orthogonal projection onto a null space
A = [1 2 -1 3;
     2 4  1 9;
     3 6  0 12];

K = [-2 -4;
      1  0;
      0 -1;
      0  1];

% Orthogonal projector onto ker(A)
P_kernel = K * ((K.'*K)\K.');

fprintf('||P_kernel^2-P_kernel|| = %.3e\n', ...
    norm(P_kernel^2-P_kernel));

fprintf('||P_kernel^T-P_kernel|| = %.3e\n', ...
    norm(P_kernel.'-P_kernel));

fprintf('||A*P_kernel|| = %.3e\n', ...
    norm(A*P_kernel));


%% 5. SPD matrices and spectral decomposition
Aspd = [2 1;
        1 2];

[Q,Lambda] = eig(Aspd);

fprintf('Eigenvalues of SPD matrix:\n');
disp(diag(Lambda));

fprintf('||A-Q*Lambda*Q^T|| = %.3e\n', ...
    norm(Aspd-Q*Lambda*Q.'));

x = [1; 0];

rho = (x.'*Aspd*x)/(x.'*x);
fprintf('Rayleigh quotient: %.8f\n', rho);

% Cholesky factorization (upper triangular R)
R = chol(Aspd);

fprintf('||A-R^T*R|| = %.3e\n', ...
    norm(Aspd-R.'*R));


%% 6. Least squares and normal equations
Als = [1 0;
       0 1;
       1 1];

b = [1; 2; 4];

% MATLAB backslash uses a suitable numerical solver
xls = Als \ b;

r = b-Als*xls;

fprintf('Least-squares solution:\n');
disp(xls);

fprintf('Residual:\n');
disp(r);

fprintf('||A^T*r|| = %.3e\n', ...
    norm(Als.'*r));

% Compare against the normal-equation solution
x_normal = (Als.'*Als)\(Als.'*b);

fprintf('||x_ls-x_normal|| = %.3e\n', ...
    norm(xls-x_normal));


%% 7. Rank-deficient minimum-norm least squares
Arank = [1 1;
         2 2];

brank = [1; 0];

x_min = pinv(Arank)*brank;

fprintf('Minimum-norm solution:\n');
disp(x_min);

fprintf('Kernel orthogonality: %.3e\n', ...
    abs([1 -1]*x_min));


%% 8. Finite-element stiffness matrix
Kfe = [6 -3;
      -3  6];

bfe = [1/3; 1/3];

cfe = Kfe\bfe;

fprintf('FE nodal values:\n');
disp(cfe);

fprintf('Smallest stiffness eigenvalue: %.8f\n', ...
    min(eig(Kfe)));


%% 9. Generalized eigenproblem
Kgen = diag([2, 6]);
Mgen = diag([2, 1]);

[V,D] = eig(Kgen,Mgen);

fprintf('Generalized eigenvalues:\n');
disp(diag(D));

T = Mgen\Kgen;

fprintf('M-self-adjointness residual: %.3e\n', ...
    norm(T.'*Mgen-Mgen*T));


%% 10. Rayleigh-Ritz in a one-dimensional subspace
q = [1; 1]/sqrt(3);  % M-normalized for M=diag(2,1)

theta = q.'*Kgen*q;

r = Kgen*q-theta*Mgen*q;

fprintf('Ritz value: %.8f\n', theta);
fprintf('Galerkin residual orthogonality: %.3e\n', ...
    abs(q.'*r));
```

### Interpretation of the laboratory {#sec-module-c-computational-laboratory-matlab-interpretation-of-the-laboratory}

The most important observations are not the individual numerical answers, but the relationships they verify.

| Experiment               | Mathematical structure to recognize                                         |
| ------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Riesz representation     | $f(x)=\langle x,a_f\rangle_G$, with $a_f=G^{-1}c$                   |
| Weighted adjoint         | $\langle Ax,y\rangle_{G_W}=\langle x,A^{*_{G_V,G_W}}y\rangle_{G_V}$ |
| Orthogonal projection    | Idempotence, self-adjointness, and best approximation                       |
| Kernel projection        | $\operatorname{im}P=\ker A$, with $P^2=P=P^T$                       |
| SPD matrix               | Positive eigenvalues, Cholesky factorization, and spectral decomposition    |
| Least squares            | The residual belongs to $\ker A^T$                                      |
| Minimum-norm solution    | The selected solution belongs to $(\ker A)^\perp$                       |
| Finite elements          | A coercive energy form leads to an SPD stiffness matrix                     |
| Generalized eigenproblem | Self-adjointness in a weighted inner product                                |
| Rayleigh–Ritz            | The approximate eigenpair residual annihilates the trial subspace           |

For larger numerical experiments, avoid using explicit matrix inverses merely because they appear in mathematical formulas.

For example, solve

$$
Ga=c
$$

using a suitable factorization instead of forming $G^{-1}$.

Similarly, solve least-squares problems using QR or SVD-based methods rather than explicitly forming normal equations when conditioning is a concern.

This distinction between **the mathematical characterization of a solution** and **a stable computational implementation** is a recurring theme of numerical linear algebra.

## Final synthesis — What Module C establishes {#sec-module-c-final-synthesis-what-module-c-establishes}

Module C has added geometric structure to the algebraic framework developed in Modules A and B.

The central relationship is

$$
\boxed{ \begin{gathered}
  \text{Algebraic dual space }V^*\\
  \updownarrow\quad\text{Riesz representation}\\
  \text{Inner-product space }V
\end{gathered} }
$$

Through this identification, the dual map becomes the adjoint, and annihilators correspond to orthogonal complements.

This leads to orthogonal decompositions and the numerical algorithms that exploit them.

### The conceptual chain {#sec-module-c-final-synthesis-what-module-c-establishes-the-conceptual-chain}

**Inner products**

$\langle x,y\rangle$ — Lengths, angles, orthogonality

**Riesz representation and adjoints**

$f(x)=\langle x,a_f\rangle$ — Covectors represented by vectors

**Orthogonal decompositions and projections**

$V=U\oplus^\perp U^\perp$ — Best approximation and least squares

**Self-adjointness and positive definiteness**

$T=T^*,\qquad\langle Tx,x\rangle>0$ — Real spectrum, orthogonal eigenspaces, and energy geometry

**Spectral and variational numerical methods**

Least squares · Galerkin approximation · Rayleigh–Ritz · Chebyshev filtering

### Important relationships to retain {#sec-module-c-final-synthesis-what-module-c-establishes-important-relationships-to-retain}

| Concept                  | Main result                                      | Interpretation                          |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------- |
| Inner product            | $\langle x,y\rangle_G=x^TGy$                 | Defines geometry                        |
| Gram matrix              | $G_{ij}=\langle v_i,v_j\rangle$             | Coordinate representation of geometry   |
| Riesz theorem            | $f(x)=\langle x,a_f\rangle$                  | Represents functionals by vectors       |
| Adjoint                  | $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,T^*y\rangle$ | Pulls output measurements backward      |
| Weighted adjoint         | $A^{*_{G_V,G_W}}=G_V^{-1}A^TG_W$           | Adjoint in non-Euclidean geometry       |
| Fundamental subspaces    | $\operatorname{im}T^*=(\ker T)^\perp$       | Algebraic duality becomes orthogonality |
| Orthogonal projection    | $P^2=P=P^*$                                 | Closest-point approximation             |
| Self-adjointness         | $T=T^*$                                     | Symmetry relative to the inner product  |
| Positive definiteness    | $\langle Tx,x\rangle>0$                      | Strictly positive quadratic energy      |
| Normal equations         | $A^T(Ax-b)=0$                                | Least-squares residual orthogonality    |
| Galerkin orthogonality   | $a(u-u_h,v_h)=0$                             | Best approximation in an energy norm    |
| Generalized eigenproblem | $Kx=\lambda Mx$                              | Spectral theory in a weighted geometry  |
| Rayleigh–Ritz            | $Q^TAQy=\theta y$                            | Projected eigenvalue approximation      |

### Final mastery checklist {#sec-module-c-final-synthesis-what-module-c-establishes-final-mastery-checklist}

Before beginning Module D, aim to be able to reconstruct the principal results independently and explain how they connect.

- [ ] Prove Cauchy–Schwarz and explain how an inner product induces norm and distance.
- [ ] Construct Gram matrices and explain why SPD matrices define inner products.
- [ ] Prove finite-dimensional Riesz representation and calculate weighted Riesz representatives.
- [ ] Derive adjoints from Riesz representation and compute weighted adjoints.
- [ ] Prove the fundamental orthogonality identities involving kernels, images, and adjoints.
- [ ] Construct orthogonal projectors, prove their best-approximation property, and distinguish them from oblique projections.
- [ ] Explain self-adjointness, the spectral theorem, positive definiteness, and the Rayleigh quotient.
- [ ] Derive least-squares normal equations and the minimum-norm solution characterization.
- [ ] Explain the role of Riesz representation, energy norms, and Galerkin orthogonality in a PDE approximation.
- [ ] Derive the Rayleigh–Ritz equations and explain the connection to generalized eigenproblems and polynomial filtering.

## Transition to Module D — Spectral theory {#sec-module-c-transition-to-module-d-spectral-theory}

Module C has introduced the essential geometry of self-adjoint operators and the spectral theorem.

Module D will build on these results to study spectral theory systematically.

In particular, we will investigate invariant subspaces, spectral decomposition, the Rayleigh quotient, Rayleigh–Ritz approximation, singular value decomposition, spectral projections, and the behavior of eigenvalues and eigenspaces under perturbations.

The central transition is from understanding the geometry of an operator to understanding how its spectrum organizes the entire space.

For a Hermitian matrix,

$$
A=Q\Lambda Q^H.
$$

This decomposition means that the action of $A$ can be understood through independent orthogonal spectral directions.

That leads directly to methods for identifying selected eigenvalues and eigenspaces.

In particular, a polynomial filter satisfies

$$
p(A)=Qp(\Lambda)Q^H.
$$

Thus the same spectral decomposition that explains the geometry of a self-adjoint operator also explains the mechanism of Chebyshev-filtered subspace iteration.

The subsequent numerical questions concern how accurately the desired invariant subspaces can be approximated, how residuals and spectral gaps control approximation quality, and how finite-precision operations affect convergence.

**The main achievement of Module C is to understand that orthogonality, adjoints, projections, positive definiteness, and spectral geometry are not isolated constructions. They arise when the algebraic theory of linear maps and duality is enriched by an inner product.**

That is the foundation for the spectral and numerical methods developed in Modules D and E.
